## Load packages

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(dplyr)
library(car)
library(MASS)

# Including my traditional diagnostics package...  See the following for details:
```

## Load the Data

```{r}
#Load the data
ed_data <- read.csv("final_data.csv")

#Remove entries without median debt reported, and
# turn it into numerical data.
ed_data <- ed_data |> subset(DEBT_MDN != "PS")
ed_data$DEBT_MDN <- as.numeric(ed_data$DEBT_MDN)

# Clean up all factors which were imported as integers.
ed_data$CONTROL.x <- as.factor(ed_data$CONTROL.x)
ed_data$REGION <- as.factor(ed_data$REGION)
ed_data$HIGHDEG <-as.factor(ed_data$HIGHDEG)
ed_data$PREDDEG <- as.factor(ed_data$PREDDEG)
ed_data$NUMBRANCH <- as.factor(ed_data$NUMBRANCH)
ed_data$MAIN.x <-as.factor(ed_data$MAIN.x)
ed_data$SCH_DEG <- as.factor(ed_data$SCH_DEG)

# Turn all numeric data that got read as strings
# back into numerical data, changing NA values to
# zero for simplicity.
cols_to_convert <- c(
  "DEATH_YR8_RT",
  "COMP_ORIG_YR8_RT",
  "COMP_4YR_TRANS_YR8_RT",
  "PELL_COMP_4YR_TRANS_YR8_RT",
  "PELL_WDRAW_ORIG_YR8_RT",
  "NOPELL_WDRAW_ORIG_YR8_RT",
  "NOT1STGEN_COMP_4YR_TRANS_YR2_RT",
  "FIRSTGEN_COMP_ORIG_YR2_RT",
  "DEBT_MDN",
  "CREDDESC",
  "DEBT_ALL_STGP_ANY_MEAN",
  "BBRR1_FED_UG_DFLT"
)

new_ed_data <- ed_data %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(cols_to_convert), ~ {
    x <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(.x))
    replace(x, is.na(x), 0)
  }))

# Now center our data. Since our original data had many character columns that should have been numeric, we must use the new_ed_data
centered_ed_data <- new_ed_data
numeric_cols <- sapply(centered_ed_data, is.numeric)
centered_ed_data[numeric_cols] <- lapply(centered_ed_data[numeric_cols],
                                         scale, scale = FALSE)
normalized_ed_data <- new_ed_data %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~as.vector(scale(.))))
rm(numeric_cols) #bruh why
```


## 1. Multiple regression models (10 pts)

At least two candidate models with several predictors are fit. Coefficients are interpreted correctly, holding the other predictors fixed. Categorical predictors are coded and interpreted correctly.

### Model 1

Our first model is going to be the full model using the raw data for increased interpretability, minus four predictors, `CITY`, which we mostly just kept because it could be fun to look at the projected earnings later, and  `CREDDESC`, which is entirely zeros, meaning we cannot use it. The last predictor we removed was `OPEID6`, which is the unique identifier for each college, which we wanted to remove so if colleges change over time, our models adjust more, rather than hardcoding the mean for each college. The last predictor we removed was `CONTROL.x`, which is exactly the same as `CONTROL.y` but coded as integers rather than the categorical variable. We still have 49 other predictors, so we are not lacking predictors.

To interpret a few of the predictors, we have the beta value associated with `ADM_RATE_ALL` is `2.903e+03`, which means that if the normalized admission rate of the school you went to increases by 1, holding all else equal, then the median earnings of a student from that schools median income increases by `2.903e+03`. Note it is more applicable to say if the school acceptance rate of the school you attended increases by 1 percent (.01), then the predicted income of a graduate is `2.903`. 

Another predictor to interpret is the beta value associated with `DEBT_MDN`, or the median original amount of the loan principal upon entering repayment of the school, which is `-1.460e-01`. Thus we have for every additional dollar of debt the median of your school, then the median earnings of the median earnings of graduates working and not enrolled 4 year after completing decreases by `.146`.

The last predictor we will interpret is the beta value associated with `CONTROL.y`, which is Control of institution, either public, private nonprofit, or private for profit. Since this is a categorical variable, it gets dummy coded. A beta value associated with `CONTROL.yPrivate, nonprofit` of `1.111e+03  5.100e+03` tells us that the median earnings of a graduates 4 years after graduating a private, nonprofit university is `1.111e+03` more than median earnings of graduates 4 years after graduating a Private for profit school. And a beta value associated with `CONTROL.yPublic` of `1.082e+03` tells us  the median earnings of a graduates 4 years after graduating a public university is `1.082e+03` more than median earnings of graduates 4 years after graduating a Private for profit school.



```{r}
model_1 <- lm(EARN_MDN_4YR ~ .-CITY-CREDDESC-OPEID6-CONTROL.x, data = new_ed_data)
summary(model_1)
```


### Model 2

Our next model is a more refined model, only using the statistically significant terms, along with statistically significant interaction terms. 

#### Polynomial Terms

The way we chose these terms is we would fit models and try different interaction and polynomial terms, and if there statistically significant predictors, we would keep them, and if not, we would remove them and try something else. For terms with very small p-values, which tell us given $\beta=0$, what is the probability that our data is at least this spread out, is very small, meaning the null model is likely wrong and there is some relationship, we chose to fit some polynomial terms, including `C150_4_WHITE` and `UGDS_WHITE`, both degree 2 to help with interpretability and because higher order polynomial terms were not as statistically significant. 

`C150_4_WHITE` is Completion rate for first-time, full-time students at four-year institutions (150% of expected time to completion) for white students. Completing college is likely a good predictor of earnings after college, so it makes sense this term is statistically significant, and it could be nonlinear. We had 4 versions of the `C150_4` terms, and chose the completion rate for white students because it had the smallest p value in the full model. 

We did a similar thing for `UGDS_WHITE`, which is the proportion of students that are white. We suspected that the data was nonlinear, and wanted to investigate it as a polynomial. 

#### Interaction Terms

We also looked at a few interaction terms. The `PCIP51` and `PCIP52` terms are "Percentage of degrees awarded in Health Professions And Related Programs" and 
"Percentage of degrees awarded in Business, Management, Marketing, And Related Support Services." Our "full" model had 4 of these terms, out of the 52 our dataset had. The two we chose had the most statistical significance, but we suspected that they interacted since other degrees exist, and degree type likely impacts earnings, so we are measuring other degrees. 

Another group of interaction terms we got was `AVGFACSAL`, `DEBT_ALL_STGP_ANY_MEAN`, and `DEBT_MDN`, which are average faculty salary, Average Stafford and Grad PLUS loan debt disbursed at all institutions, and The median original amount of the loan principal upon entering repayment. All of these terms were statistically significant, and we were curious if they interacted, and if so how much they interacted, since staff salary may correlate with increased costs and higher debt. We were also curious how mean debt interacted with median debt, since mean is more impacted by heavy tails and we wanted some way to measure distribution of student debt. 

#### Interpretation

To interpret what a few of these values mean, we have the beta value associate with `ADM_RATE_ALL` is `4.897e+03`. Since this is not a part of any interaction terms or polynomial terms, we know that if the admission rate of the college increased by 1 percent, then the predicted Median earnings of graduates working and not enrolled 4 year after completing would increase `48.97`. 

The beta value associated with `DEBT_MDN` is `-1.891e-01`, which means that the linear component of the `DEBT_MDN` is `-1.891e-01`. 

The beta value assoicated with `AVGFACSAL:DEBT_MDN`, the interaction between these two predictors is `-8.150e-05` which means 

AVGFACSAL:DEBT_MDN                      -8.150e-05  1.549e-05  -5.262
DEBT_ALL_STGP_ANY_MEAN:DEBT_MDN          2.350e-05  3.510e-06   6.694


```{r}
model_2 <- lm(EARN_MDN_4YR~MAIN.x  + ADM_RATE_ALL+poly(C150_4_WHITE,2) + (PCIP51 + PCIP52)^2 + poly(UGDS_WHITE,2) + INEXPFTE + (AVGFACSAL + DEBT_ALL_STGP_ANY_MEAN + DEBT_MDN)^2 + COMP_ORIG_YR8_RT+ (DEATH_YR8_RT+PELL_COMP_4YR_TRANS_YR8_RT)^2 + NOPELL_WDRAW_ORIG_YR8_RT+ DISTANCE + (SATVRMID + SATMTMID)^2 ,data=centered_ed_data)
summary(model_2)
```


### Model 3

```{r}
# Find the lm for the unshifted data, so we can get a boxcox model.
model_3_unshifted <- lm(
  EARN_MDN_4YR ~ (TUITIONFEE_IN + CONTROL.x + ADM_RATE_ALL)^2
  + PREDDEG + HIGHDEG + C150_4 + C150_4:ADM_RATE_ALL + DEBT_MDN,
  data = ed_data
)
# Generate boxcox model, and show plot.  Then, transform data.
bc3 <- boxcox(model_3_unshifted)
#bc3
bc3$x[which.max(bc3$y)]
m3_transformed_data = ed_data
# Apply boxcox transform.
m3_transformed_data$EARN_MDN_4YR = ((ed_data$EARN_MDN_4YR^bc3$x[which.max(bc3$y)] - 1)/bc3$x[which.max(bc3$y)])
# Do some cleaning up.
rm(model_3_unshifted)
rm(bc3)
# Now center the data.
centered_m3_data <- m3_transformed_data
numeric_cols <- sapply(m3_transformed_data, is.numeric)
centered_m3_data[numeric_cols] <- lapply(centered_m3_data[numeric_cols],
                                         scale, scale = FALSE)
rm(numeric_cols)
# And finally, generate the actual model and give the summary.
model_3 <- lm(
  EARN_MDN_4YR ~ (TUITIONFEE_IN + CONTROL.x + ADM_RATE_ALL)^2
  + PREDDEG + HIGHDEG + C150_4 + C150_4:ADM_RATE_ALL + DEBT_MDN,
  data = centered_m3_data
)
summary(model_3)
```

For our third, model, we took a more hand-built approach. We included in-state tuition fee, institution type (public, private non-profit, or private for-profit), and admission rate, as well as all degree two interaction terms between these; predicted degree accomplishment, highest degree achieved, completion rate, median debt, and the interaction term between completion rate and institution admission rate.

Preemptively, we examine the Box-Cox plot, and find that a transform of the data is needed. This is backed up by (TODO) the QQ-plot not being very linear, and the histogram of residuals not following a normal distribution. After this transform, we center our data to eliminate non-essential contributions of interaction and polynomial terms with the base variables.

After this transform, we label our variables as follows: $Y$ as our transformed and centered version of four-year median earnings, $X_1$ as our centered in-state tuition, $X_2$ as our indicator for being a private nonprofit institution, $X_3$ as our indicator for being a private for-profit institution, $X_4$ as our centered admission rate as a decimal, $X_5$ as our indicator for predicted degree, $X_6$ and $X_7$ as our indicators for the various options of highest degree offered (master's and doctoral), $X_8$ as our centered graduation rate (TODO, check this), and $X_9$ as our centered median debt. This gives us the following model:

$$ Y = 10^{-3} ( -7.157+ 2.425 \cdot 10^{-4} X_1 -4.087 X_2 + 0.7901 X_3 - 4.019 X_4 + 1.016 X_5 + 7.124 X_6 \\
+ 8.216 X_7 + 3.905 X_8 - 2.851 \cdot 10^{-5} - 1.368 \cdot 10^{-4} X_1 X_2 - 5.906 \cdot 10^{-4} X_1 X_3 \\
- 7.555 \cdot 10^{-5} X_1 X_4 + 5.558 X_2 X_4 + 5.190 X_3 X_4 - 6.031 X_4 X_8 )$$

Here, we factor the $10^{-3}$ term out to save space.

To interpret this model, we begin by noting that in this model, the values of $Y$ are rather small, due both to the Box-Cox transform and the centering. As such, we go in with the knowledge that each variable is, itself, going to be rather small.

For the intercept, $-7.157 \cdot 10^{-3}$, we know that this is the contribution to $Y$ in the case that a school is numerically average, with each of our indicators as zero. This is notably not the same as being an average university. The indicated $p$-value shows that this is likely non-zero.

For the coefficient of $X_1$, the in-state tuition, is $2.425 \cdot 10^{-7}$. The smaller coefficient here makes sense, as in-state tuition tend to be measured in thousands of dollars. The interpretation here is that the direct (linear) contribution of in-state tuition is approximately $2.425 \cdot 10^{-7}$, meaning that the higher the in-state tuition of a university, the higher your median income four years after graduation will be. The $p$-value of this coefficient is low, indicating that it could very reasonably be zero. However, we include it as one of the interaction terms including this term has a higher $p$-value.

For the coefficient of $X_2$, we find that for private nonprofit institutions, the transformed and centered median income decreases by $4.087 \cdot 10^{-3}$. The $p$-value for this coefficient is also low, so it could reasonably be zero. However, we include it as the indicator for the other option is very likely non-zero.

For the coefficient of $X_3$, we find that for private for-profit institutions, the expected contribution to the transformed and adjusted median income increases by $7.901 \cdot 10^{-4}$. From the associated $t$-test and $p$-value, we know that this is very likely not zero. As such, we keep both it, and the associated indicator $X_2$.

For the coefficient of $X_4$, we find that for every $1$ your decimal expression of acceptance rate increases from the mean national acceptance rate, the transformed and shifted four-year median income after graduation goes down by $4.019 \cdot 10^{-3}$. For a more readable interpretation, the more selective an institution, the higher the median pay is likely to be four years after graduation. The associated $t$-test tells us that this effect may not actually be present at all, and this coefficient may actually be zero.

### Model 3

Here, we include degree two interaction terms between in-state tuition, institution type, and admission rate. This is because the effect of in-state tuition can be mitigated by private institutions waiving tuition, in-state tuition can often be waived by higher admittance requirements (reflected by admission rate), and institution type and admission rate together can tell us how selective the institution is, often indicating how well perceived the institution is in the job market.

There is also room for C150_4 to have interaction terms with practically every other variable present, as drop-out rate is a very useful indicator of median pay after graduation. Given the nature of graduation rate and admittance criteria, they will likely have interaction in that the more strict the admittance criteria, the higher the graduation rate will likely be. As such, we try to account for how this effects pay by including an interaction term.

The remaining items: median debt, predicted degree, and highest degree received, all indicate base-line requirements for most students at these institutions, and help us account for what the average student at these institutions look like.
